relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: A prophetic word reaches the dynasty Baasha built through massacre.
The one raised from dust has reproduced Jeroboam's system.
Judgment promises to sweep away another royal house.
Unburied bodies and scavenging animals again become the language of political condemnation.
The official record remembers Baasha's power beyond the oracle.
He dies, is buried, and transfers rule to Elah.
The prophet condemns both imitation of Jeroboam and the killing by which Baasha rose.
Elah's reign lasts two years.
A chariot commander plans assassination while the king drinks in a trusted official's house.
Zimri kills Elah and takes the throne.
He immediately exterminates Baasha's male kin and political circle.
The massacre is narrated as prophecy fulfilled.
Dynastic violence is placed beside religious failure.
Elah's short record closes.
Zimri rules only seven days while the army remains at siege.
The camp answers the coup by crowning its commander Omri.
The army turns from Gibbethon and besieges its own capital.
Zimri sees defeat, burns the palace over himself, and dies within it.
The narrator makes his death a moral conclusion, but compassion refuses to turn suicide into spectacle or doctrine.
The archive records conspiracy beyond the seven-day summary.
Israel divides again between two claimants.
Omri's faction prevails, Tibni dies, and military power becomes monarchy.
Omri begins a twelve-year reign.
A purchased hill becomes Samaria, named after its former owner.
The new capital does not make the new ruler just.
Omri continues the religious system of Jeroboam.
His might survives in another record.
Omri is buried in Samaria and Ahab inherits the throne.
Ahab rules from the new capital for twenty-two years.
The narrative marks him as surpassing previous royal failure.
He marries Jezebel and establishes Sidonian royal religion in Israel; the decision remains his as king.
A temple and altar for Baal rise in Samaria.
An Asherah joins the royal sanctuary system.
Jericho's rebuilding is bracketed by the deaths of Hiel's firstborn and youngest son, a horrifying cost no city should require.

contemplative_note: The chapter moves through assassination, massacre, siege, self-inflicted death, civil conflict, capital building, and child loss. The throne changes hands repeatedly while violence reproduces itself. Stability without mercy is merely a pause between funerals.
